entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8226"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <div sID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.11">So 3:1-11</reference>.<div eID="gen12934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12935" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8226"/><hi type="bold">1. By night--</hi>literally, "By nights." Continuation of the longing for the dawn of the Messiah (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.6">Psa 130:6</reference>; Mal 4:2). The spiritual desertion here (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">3:5</reference>) is not due to indifference, as in <reference osisRef="Song.5.2-Song.5.8">So 5:2-8</reference>. "As nights and dews are better for flowers than a continual sun, so Christ's absence (at times) giveth sap to humility, and putteth an edge on hunger, and furnisheth a fair field to faith to put forth itself" [Rutherford]. Contrast <reference osisRef="Song.1.13">So 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Psa 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">7</reference>.<div eID="gen12935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on ... bed--</hi>the secret of her failure (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.7">Is 64:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">Jr 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Ho 7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen12936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loveth--</hi>no want of sincerity, but of diligence, which she now makes up for by leaving her bed to seek Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.2">Psa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">63:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.9">Is 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.17">Joh 20:17</reference>). Four times (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.4">So 3:1-4</reference>) she calls Jesus Christ, "Him whom my soul loveth," designating Him as absent; language of desire: "He loved me," would be language of present fruition (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>). In questioning the watchmen (<reference osisRef="Song.3.3">So 3:3</reference>), she does not even name Him, so full is her heart of Him. Having found Him at dawn (for throughout He is the morning), she charges the daughters not to abridge by intrusion the period of His stay. Compare as to the thoughtful seeking for Jesus Christ in the time of John the Baptist, in vain at first, but presently after successful (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.15-Luke.3.22">Lu 3:15-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.19-John.1.34">Joh 1:19-34</reference>).<div eID="gen12937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him not--</hi>Oh, for such honest dealings with ourselves (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.14">Pr 25:14</reference>; Jude 12)! <div eID="gen12938" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 3 So 3:1-11 . 1. By night-- literally, "By nights." Continuation of the longing for the dawn of the Messiah ( So 2:17 ; Psa 130:6 ; Mal 4:2). The spiritual desertion here ( So 2:17 ; 3:5 ) is not due to indifference, as in So 5:2-8 . "As nights and dews are better for flowers than a continual sun, so Christ's absence (at times) giveth sap to humility, and putteth an edge on hunger, and furnisheth a fair field to faith to put forth itself" [Rutherford]. Contrast So 1:13 ; Psa 30:6 , 7 . on ... bed-- the secret of her failure ( Is 64:7 ; Jr 29:13 ; Am 6:1 , 4 ; Ho 7:14 ). loveth-- no want of sincerity, but of diligence, which she now makes up for by leaving her bed to seek Him ( Psa 22:2 ; 63:8 ; Is 26:9 ; Joh 20:17 ). Four times ( So 3:1-4 ) she calls Jesus Christ, "Him whom my soul loveth," designating Him as absent; language of desire: "He loved me," would be language of present fruition ( Re 1:5 ). In questioning the watchmen ( So 3:3 ), she does not even name Him, so full is her heart of Him. Having found Him at dawn (for throughout He is the morning), she charges the daughters not to abridge by intrusion the period of His stay. Compare as to the thoughtful seeking for Jesus Christ in the time of John the Baptist, in vain at first, but presently after successful ( Lu 3:15-22 ; Joh 1:19-34 ). found him not-- Oh, for such honest dealings with ourselves ( Pr 25:14 ; Jude 12)!

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8227"/><div sID="gen12939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8227"/><hi type="bold">2. Wholly awake for God (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.18-Luke.14.20">Lu 14:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>). "An honest resolution is often to (the doing of) duty, like a needle that draws the thread after it" [Durham]. Not a mere wish, that counts not the cost--</hi>to leave her easy bed, and wander in the dark night seeking Him (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.4">Pr 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.30">Mt 21:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.27-Luke.14.33">Lu 14:27-33</reference>).<div eID="gen12939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the city--</hi>Jerusalem, literally (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.5">Mt 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.19">Joh 1:19</reference>), and spiritually the Church here (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>), in glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broad ways--</hi>open spaces at the gates of Eastern cities, where the public assembled for business. So, the assemblies of worshippers (<reference osisRef="Song.8.2">So 8:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.8.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20-Prov.1.23">Pr 1:20-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>). She had in her first awakening shrunk from them, seeking Jesus Christ alone; but she was desired to seek the footsteps of the flock (<reference osisRef="Song.1.8">So 1:8</reference>), so now in her second trial she goes forth to them of herself. "The more the soul grows in grace, and the less it leans on ordinances, the more it prizes and profits by them" [Moody Stuart] (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen12941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him not--</hi>Nothing short of Jesus Christ can satisfy her (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.10">Job 23:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>, 2). <div eID="gen12942" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8229"/><div sID="gen12945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8229"/>4. Jesus Christ is generally "found" near the watchmen and means of grace; but they are not Himself; the star that points to Beth-lehem is not the Sun that has risen there; she hastens past the guideposts to the goal [Moody Stuart]. Not even angels could satisfy Mary, instead of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.20.11-John.20.16">Joh 20:11-16</reference>).<div eID="gen12945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">found him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1-Hos.6.3">Ho 6:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44-Matt.13.46">Mt 13:44-46</reference>).<div eID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">held him, &c.--</hi>willing to be held; not willing, if not held (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Ge 32:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.9">Mt 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.28">Lu 24:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.11">Re 3:11</reference>). "As a little weeping child will hold its mother fast, not because it is stronger than she, but because her bowels constrain her not to leave it; so Jesus Christ yearning over the believer cannot go, because He will not" [Durham]. In <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference> it is He who leads the bride into His chambers; here it is she who leads Him into her mother's. There are times when the grace of Jesus Christ seems to draw us to Him; and others, when we with strong cries draw Him to us and ours. In the East one large apartment often serves for the whole family; so the bride here speaks of her mother's apartment and her own together. The mention of the "mother" excludes impropriety, and imparts the idea of heavenly love, pure as a sister's, while ardent as a bride's; hence the frequent title, "my sister--spouse." Our mother after the Spirit, is the Church, the new Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="John.3.5-John.3.8">Joh 3:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.19">Ga 4:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">26</reference>); for her we ought to pray continually (<reference osisRef="Eph.3.14-Eph.3.19">Ep 3:14-19</reference>), also for the national Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.1">Ro 10:1</reference>), also for the human family, which is our mother and kindred after the flesh; these our mother's children have evilly treated us (<reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>); but, like our Father, we are to return good for evil (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">45</reference>), and so bring Jesus Christ home to them (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.12">1Pe 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen12947" type="x-p"/>

So <reference osisRef="Song.2.7">So 2:7</reference>; but there it was for the non-interruption of her own fellowship with Jesus Christ that she was anxious; here it is for the not grieving of the Holy Ghost, on the part of the daughters of Jerusalem. Jealously avoid levity, heedlessness, and offenses which would mar the gracious work begun in others (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.7">Mt 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.42">Ac 2:42</reference>, 43; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canticle III.--</hi>(So 3:6-5:1)--The Bridegroom with the Bride.<div eID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> Historically, the ministry of Jesus Christ on earth. <div eID="gen12950" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8231"/><div sID="gen12951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8231"/>6. New scene (<reference osisRef="Song.3.6-Song.3.11">So 3:6-11</reference>). The friends of the Bridegroom see a cortege approach. His palanquin and guard.<div eID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cometh out--</hi>rather, "up from"; the wilderness was lower than Jerusalem [Maurer].<div eID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pillars of smoke--</hi>from the perfumes burned around Him and His bride. Image from Israel and the tabernacle (answering to "bed," <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>) marching through the desert with the pillar of smoke by day and fire by night (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">Ex 14:20</reference>), and the pillars of smoke ascending from the altars of incense and of atonement; so Jesus Christ's righteousness, atonement, and ever-living intercession. Balaam, the last representative of patriarchism, was required to curse the Jewish Church, just as it afterwards would not succumb to Christianity without a struggle (<reference osisRef="Num.22.41">Nu 22:41</reference>), but he had to bless in language like that here (<reference osisRef="Num.24.5">Nu 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.24.6">6</reference>). Angels too joyfully ask the same question, when Jesus Christ with the tabernacle of His body (answering to "His bed," <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, "dwelt," Greek "tabernacled," <reference osisRef="John.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>) ascends into heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.8-Ps.24.10">Psa 24:8-10</reference>); also when they see His glorious bride with Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.18">Psa 68:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.13-Rev.7.17">Re 7:13-17</reference>). Encouragement to her; amid the darkest trials (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1">So 3:1</reference>), she is still on the road to glory (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">So 3:11</reference>) in a palanquin "paved with love" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.10">So 3:10</reference>); she is now in soul spiritually "coming," exhaling the sweet graces, faith, love, joy, peace, prayer, and praise; (the fire is lighted within, the "smoke" is seen without, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>); it is in the desert of trial (<reference osisRef="Song.3.1-Song.3.3">So 3:1-3</reference>) she gets them; she is the "merchant" buying from Jesus Christ without money or price (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>); just as myrrh and frankincense are got, not in Egypt, but in the Arabian sands and the mountains of Palestine. Hereafter she shall "come" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.6">So 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.3.11">11</reference>) in a glorified body, too (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>). Historically, Jesus Christ returning from the wilderness, full of the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.1">Lu 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.14">14</reference>). The same, "Who is this," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen12953" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 6. New scene ( So 3:6-11 ). The friends of the Bridegroom see a cortege approach. His palanquin and guard. cometh out-- rather, "up from"; the wilderness was lower than Jerusalem [Maurer]. pillars of smoke-- from the perfumes burned around Him and His bride. Image from Israel and the tabernacle (answering to "bed," So 3:7 ) marching through the desert with the pillar of smoke by day and fire by night ( Ex 14:20 ), and the pillars of smoke ascending from the altars of incense and of atonement; so Jesus Christ's righteousness, atonement, and ever-living intercession. Balaam, the last representative of patriarchism, was required to curse the Jewish Church, just as it afterwards would not succumb to Christianity without a struggle ( Nu 22:41 ), but he had to bless in language like that here ( Nu 24:5 , 6 ). Angels too joyfully ask the same question, when Jesus Christ with the tabernacle of His body (answering to "His bed," So 3:7 ; Joh 1:14 , "dwelt," Greek "tabernacled," Joh 2:21 ) ascends into heaven ( Psa 24:8-10 ); also when they see His glorious bride with Him ( Psa 68:18 ; Re 7:13-17 ). Encouragement to her; amid the darkest trials ( So 3:1 ), she is still on the road to glory ( So 3:11 ) in a palanquin "paved with love" ( So 3:10 ); she is now in soul spiritually "coming," exhaling the sweet graces, faith, love, joy, peace, prayer, and praise; (the fire is lighted within, the "smoke" is seen without, Ac 4:13 ); it is in the desert of trial ( So 3:1-3 ) she gets them; she is the "merchant" buying from Jesus Christ without money or price ( Is 55:1 ; Re 3:18 ); just as myrrh and frankincense are got, not in Egypt, but in the Arabian sands and the mountains of Palestine. Hereafter she shall "come" ( So 3:6 , 11 ) in a glorified body, too ( Php 3:21 ). Historically, Jesus Christ returning from the wilderness, full of the Holy Ghost ( Lu 4:1 , 14 ). The same, "Who is this," &c. ( Is 63:1 , 5 ).

His palanquin and guard. cometh out-- rather, "up from"; the wilderness was lower than Jerusalem [Maurer]. pillars of smoke-- from the perfumes burned around Him and His bride. Image from Israel and the tabernacle (answering to "bed," So 3:7 ) marching through the desert with the pillar of smoke by day and fire by night ( Ex 14:20 ), and the pillars of smoke ascending from the altars of incense and of atonement; so Jesus Christ's righteousness, atonement, and ever-living intercession. Balaam, the last representative of patriarchism, was required to curse the Jewish Church, just as it afterwards would not succumb to Christianity without a struggle ( Nu 22:41 ), but he had to bless in language like that here ( Nu 24:5 , 6 ). Angels too joyfully ask the same question, when Jesus Christ with the tabernacle of His body (answering to "His bed," So 3:7 ; Joh 1:14 , "dwelt," Greek "tabernacled," Joh 2:21 ) ascends into heaven ( Psa 24:8-10 ); also when they see His glorious bride with Him ( Psa 68:18 ; Re 7:13-17 ). Encouragement to her; amid the darkest trials ( So 3:1 ), she is still on the road to glory ( So 3:11 ) in a palanquin "paved with love" ( So 3:10 ); she is now in soul spiritually "coming," exhaling the sweet graces, faith, love, joy, peace, prayer, and praise; (the fire is lighted within, the "smoke" is seen without, Ac 4:13 ); it is in the desert of trial ( So 3:1-3 ) she gets them; she is the "merchant" buying from Jesus Christ without money or price ( Is 55:1 ; Re 3:18 ); just as myrrh and frankincense are got, not in Egypt, but in the Arabian sands and the mountains of Palestine. Hereafter she shall "come" ( So 3:6 , 11 ) in a glorified body, too ( Php 3:21 ). Historically, Jesus Christ returning from the wilderness, full of the Holy Ghost ( Lu 4:1 , 14 ). The same, "Who is this," &c. ( Is 63:1 , 5 ).

So the temple of "cedar of Lebanon," as compared with the temporary tabernacle of shittim wood (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.6.7">6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.14">1Ki 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.15-1Kgs.6.18">6:15-18</reference>), Jesus Christ's body is the antitype, "made" by the Father for Him (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>), the wood answering to His human nature, the gold, His divine; the two being but one Christ. <div eID="gen12960" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8235"/><div sID="gen12961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8235"/><hi type="bold">10. pillars--</hi>supporting the canopy at the four corners; curtains at the side protect the person within from the sun. Pillars with silver sockets supported the veil that enclosed the holy of holies; emblem of Jesus Christ's strength (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.21">1Ki 7:21</reference>), Margin, "silver," emblem of His purity (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>); so the saints hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Re 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bottom--</hi>rather, "the back for resting or reclining on" (Vulgate and Septuagint) [Maurer]. So the floor and mercy seat, the resting-place of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">Psa 132:14</reference>) in the temple, was gold (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.30">1Ki 6:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covering--</hi>rather, "seat," as in <reference osisRef="Lev.15.9">Le 15:9</reference>. Hereafter the saints shall share His seat (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>).<div eID="gen12963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purple--</hi>the veil of the holiest, partly purple, and the purple robe put on Jesus Christ, accord with English Version, "covering." "Purple" (including scarlet and crimson) is the emblem of royalty, and of His blood; typified by the passover lamb's blood, and the wine when the twelve sat or reclined at the Lord's table.<div eID="gen12964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">paved--</hi>translated, like mosaic pavement, with the various acts and promises of love of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">16</reference>), in contrast with the tables of stone in the "midst" of the ark, covered with writings of stern command (compare <reference osisRef="John.19.13">Joh 19:13</reference>); this is all grace and love to believers, who answer to "the daughters of Jerusalem" (<reference osisRef="John.1.17">Joh 1:17</reference>). The exterior silver and gold, cedar, purple, and guards, may deter, but when the bride enters within, she rests on a pavement of love. <div eID="gen12965" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8236"/><div sID="gen12966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8236"/><hi type="bold">11. Go forth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">Mt 25:6</reference>).<div eID="gen12966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Zion--</hi>spirits of saints, and angels (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crown--</hi>nuptial (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.8-Ezek.16.12">Eze 16:8-12</reference>), (the Hebrews wore costly crowns or chaplets at weddings), and kingly (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.12">Re 19:12</reference>). The crown of thorns was once His nuptial chaplet, His blood the wedding wine cup (<reference osisRef="John.19.5">Joh 19:5</reference>). "His mother," that so crowned Him, is the human race, for He is "the Son of man," not merely the son of Mary. The same mother reconciled to Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">Mt 12:50</reference>), as the Church, travails in birth for souls, which she presents to Him as a crown (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">Php 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.10">Re 4:10</reference>). Not being ashamed to call the children brethren (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.11-Heb.2.14">He 2:11-14</reference>), He calls their mother His mother (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Re 12:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen12968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen12969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of his espousals--</hi>chiefly the final marriage, when the number of the elect is complete (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.11">Re 6:11</reference>).<div eID="gen12970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gladness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.45.15">Psa 45:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Is 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Re 19:7</reference>). Moody Stuart observes as to this Canticle (So 3:6-5:1), the center of the Book, these characteristics: (1) The bridegroom takes the chief part, whereas elsewhere the bride is the chief speaker. (2) Elsewhere He is either "King" or "Solomon"; here He is twice called "King Solomon." The bride is six times here called the "spouse"; never so before or after; also "sister" four times, and, except in the first verse of the next Canticle [So 5:2], nowhere else. (3) He and she are never separate; no absence, no complaint, which abound elsewhere, are in this Canticle. <chapter eID="Song.3"/>
